hook.explorer: Touch the apple and the light turns on!
hook.builder: Make a light that switches on when you touch a piece of fruit - no button needed.
hook.engineer: Build a Darlington pair touch switch and use fruit as the base-current path.

instruction.explorer: Put the first three-legged helper in the board.
instruction.builder: Push the first transistor in with its flat side facing you. Its three legs go into rows 20, 21 and 22.
instruction.engineer: Insert Q1 with the flat face towards you: collector to row 20, base to row 21, emitter to row 22. Check your part's pinout - 2N3904 and 2N2222 differ.

instruction.explorer: Now the second helper, just below.
instruction.builder: Push the second transistor in the same way, into rows 24, 25 and 26.
instruction.engineer: Insert Q2 identically: collector row 24, base row 25, emitter row 26.

instruction.explorer: Join the two helpers together with wires.
instruction.builder: Run a jumper from A22 to A25, and another from A20 to A24. Now the two transistors work as a team.
instruction.engineer: Wire the Darlington: Q1 emitter (row 22) to Q2 base (row 25), and tie the collectors together (row 20 to row 24).

explanation.explorer: Two helpers together are MUCH stronger than one.
explanation.builder: One transistor makes a tiny trickle about a hundred times bigger. Two in a row makes it about ten thousand times bigger. That's why fruit is enough to switch this on.
explanation.engineer: A Darlington multiplies the gains: roughly 100 x 100 = 10,000. That is exactly why a base current of tens of microamps through fruit can switch tens of milliamps through the LED.

instruction.explorer: Add the strongest brake from the middle leg down to black.
instruction.builder: Put the 1MΩ resistor from B21 to the black rail. This stops the light flickering on by itself.
instruction.engineer: Fit the 1MΩ base pull-down from Q1 base (row 21) to ground. Without it the base floats and the Darlington's huge gain makes it switch on at random.

instruction.explorer: Now the light and its little brake.
instruction.builder: Put the LED's long leg in B26 and its short leg in B29. Then put the 330Ω resistor from E29 to the black rail.
instruction.engineer: LED anode to Q2 emitter (row 26), cathode to row 29, then the 330Ω limiting resistor from row 29 to ground. Emitter follower - the LED sits in the emitter leg.

instruction.explorer: Connect the battery. The light should be OFF.
instruction.builder: Connect the battery, and run a jumper from the red rail to C20. The LED should be off. If it's on, check the 1MΩ resistor.
instruction.engineer: Power up and tie the collectors to +9V. The LED should be dark. If it glows, the base pull-down is missing or in the wrong net.

expect.engineer: Quiescent state, base held near ground.

instruction.explorer: Push two nails in the fruit. Clip a wire to each.
instruction.builder: Push two nails into the lemon about 3cm apart. Clip one to the red rail, and clip the other to C21 - the middle leg of the first transistor.
instruction.engineer: Insert two electrodes into the fruit. Clip one to +9V and the other to Q1's base net (row 21). The fruit is now the base resistor - tens of kilohms of it.

expect.explorer: THE LIGHT COMES ON! The fruit is the switch!
expect.builder: The LED lights up! The lemon is letting just enough electricity through to the middle leg to switch the whole thing on.
expect.engineer: The LED should light. The fruit passes tens of microamps into the base; the Darlington multiplies that into milliamps through the LED.

instruction.explorer: Now pull a nail out and touch it with your finger!
instruction.builder: Take the clip off the lemon and just hold the bare wire between your fingers while touching the other one. You are now the switch!
instruction.engineer: Replace the fruit with your own skin. Dry skin is megohms, which is right at the edge of what this circuit can switch - lick your finger and the LED brightens noticeably.

expect.explorer: You are part of the circuit!
expect.builder: It works with YOU in the circuit. Try a damp finger - much brighter!
expect.engineer: Brightness tracks skin resistance, which is a direct readout of the Darlington's current gain.

bigIdea.explorer: A tiny bit of electricity can control a big bit of electricity.
bigIdea.builder: A transistor is an amplifier: a trickle too small to do anything on its own can control a flow big enough to light a lamp. Two transistors together are so sensitive that a piece of fruit is enough to trigger them.
bigIdea.engineer: This is current gain. The fruit's resistance is far too high to light an LED directly - as the lemon battery experiment proved - but a Darlington's gain of about 10,000 turns those microamps into milliamps. Amplification is the whole reason transistors changed the world.

goFurther.explorer: Try other things instead of the fruit!
goFurther.builder: Swap the lemon for a banana, a pickle, a wet sponge, a chain of people holding hands. What works? What doesn't?
goFurther.engineer: Substitute different organics and rank them by resulting LED brightness - a working transconductance measurement. Log them in the Conductivity Leaderboard.

goFurther.explorer: How many people can hold hands and still work?
goFurther.builder: Get the whole family holding hands in a line, with the people on the ends holding the wires. How many people before the light goes out?
goFurther.engineer: Series-connect people and find where the total resistance exceeds what the Darlington can work with. Each person adds roughly a megohm of dry skin.
